title: About
text:
Featured Project: Across the Atlantic
Our first featured marine research project, Across the Atlantic, explores sea turtle distribution and migration patterns across the Atlantic Ocean. It uses a proposed sailing route from Freeport, Bahamas, to the Azores, Portugal, as a geographic frame to ask:

How do sea turtle migration patterns connect the Caribbean and the Atlantic Ocean?

title: About
text:
Scope and Limitations

Combined Sea Turtle Records: Our map plots all 120,718 Atlantic observations by latitude and longitude in one layer; it does not separate points by individual species, season, or individual animal track.
Proposed Sailing Route: As noted on the Home page, the red markers at Freeport and the Azores identify endpoints of a proposed sailing voyage, not a single measured turtle migration path.
Survey Effort: Dense clusters on the map reflect where sea turtles are frequently found as well as where scientific surveys and tracking programs collect the most data.

On the map below, each observation is plotted with partial transparency (alpha = 0.18). Isolated sightings appear faint, while areas with many overlapping records build into dark teal hotspots.

On the map below, each observation is plotted with partial transparency (alpha = 0.18). Isolated sightings appear faint, while areas with many overlapping records build into dark teal hotspots.

title: Migration Hotspots
section: Major Hotspots Visible in the Data
text:
Major Hotspots Visible in the Data
Across the plotted OBIS records, five main high-density regions stand out:

The Bahamas and Southeastern North America (~25°N–42°N, 82°W–70°W): One of the darkest continuous bands on the map follows the western Atlantic coast near Freeport, Bahamas (26.5°N, 78.7°W), Florida, and northward along the U.S. Atlantic shelf.
The Caribbean Sea (~10°N–20°N, 85°W–60°W): Dense island clusters and curved travel paths span the Caribbean basin, with smaller coastal concentrations continuing south toward 5°S.
Northwestern Atlantic Offshore Waters (~42°N–48°N, 50°W–40°W): A distinct offshore cluster appears northeast of the North American coast in open North Atlantic waters.
The Azores (~37°N–40°N, 31°W–24°W): In the central North Atlantic, observations cluster tightly around the Azores (37.7°N, 25.7°W), highlighting these mid-ocean islands as an active hub surrounded by deep ocean.
Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Entrance (~35°N–44°N, 10°W–10°E): Heavy shading covers the waters around the Iberian Peninsula and the entrance to the Mediterranean Sea, with connected movement tracks extending south off West Africa.

title: Migration Hotspots
text:
How to Interpret Observation Hotspots
Hotspots on a biodiversity map reflect two factors working together:

Habitat Use: Dense clusters point to productive coastal shelves, island groups, and ocean corridors where sea turtles regularly feed, nest, or travel.
Observation Effort: Because OBIS compiles scientific surveys and tracking studies, accessible coastlines and monitored island regions naturally accumulate more recorded sightings than remote open-ocean waters.

section: Following the Migration Patterns of Sea Turtles
text:
Following the Migration Patterns of Sea Turtles
This project explores sea turtle migration across the Atlantic Ocean using real tracking data.
Our journey follows a sailing route from Freeport, Bahamas, toward the Azores while exploring where sea turtles travel, how far they migrate, and how their paths connect across the ocean.

Research Question
How do sea turtle migration patterns connect the Caribbean and the Atlantic Ocean?

title: Species & Ocean Patterns
text:
The 120,718 OBIS observations in this project combine recorded sea turtle locations across the Atlantic study window (85°W to 10°E, 5°S to 65°N).
In our mapping script (migration_map.R), all sea turtle records are plotted together in a single color using latitude and longitude rather than separated by species name. While this combined dataset does not provide separate species counts on the map, it clearly shows broad ocean patterns shared across Atlantic sea turtle observations.



Combined Atlantic sea turtle geographic records from OBIS showing coastal bands, open-ocean points, and movement paths.

title: Species & Ocean Patterns
section: Ocean Patterns Visible on the Map
text:
Ocean Patterns Visible on the Map

Coastal Shelves and Open-Ocean Waters
The densest bands follow continental coastlines and island groups on both sides of the ocean. At the same time, widespread points stretch across the deep central Atlantic between Freeport, Bahamas (26.5°N, 78.7°W) and the Azores (37.7°N, 25.7°W), showing that sea turtles occupy both shallow nearshore habitats and open-ocean waters.


Distribution by Latitude
Although the study area spans from 5°S to 65°N, the vast majority of observations fall between roughly 10°N and 45°N. North of 50°N, records become sparse, matching sea turtles’ strong preference for warmer tropical, subtropical, and temperate waters.


Movement Tracks vs. Gridded Records
Looking closely at the plotted points reveals two distinct recording patterns in OBIS:

Continuous curved lines—especially clear across the Caribbean, south of the Azores, and along Europe and West Africa—which represent repeated positions along travel paths.
Evenly spaced grid dots across the central North Atlantic (~20°N–45°N), where sightings have been summarized into regular latitude-longitude grid cells.

title: Species & Ocean Patterns
section: Connecting the Caribbean and the Atlantic
text:
Connecting the Caribbean and the Atlantic
Together, these patterns address our research question. Even though the red markers at Freeport and the Azores represent a proposed sailing journey rather than a single turtle’s measured route, the continuous spread of observations across the basin shows that the Caribbean, western Atlantic coast, mid-ocean Azores, and eastern Atlantic are linked by active sea turtle presence.
